newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil leader reaffirms commitment to stability.
newsitem.headline: Brazil leader reaffirms commitment to stability.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso Wednesday reaffirmed his commitment to economic stability, vowing that the fight against inflation would not be abandoned in election year 1998.

Speaking as he sanctioned Brazil's new General Telecommunications Law and a day after nervousness over a possible devaluation wiped 8.0 percent off share prices, Cardoso also stuck his colors to the mast of fiscal prudence.

"We must always be concerned about the public accounts," the Brazilian leader said. "The whole country knows of the government's determination, and of mine personally, to balance the public accounts."

"Our fundamental commitment...is to guarantee the stability of our currency and to guarantee that salaries aren't eaten away by inflation," he added, pledging not to loosen the reins on inflation during next year's presidential election campaign.
Last year's consolidated public sector operational deficit of 3.86 percent of gross domestic product was lower than 1995's 5.0 percent of GDP shortfall. But it was still above target.

Despite the current focus on Brazil's external accounts, analysts say one of the main threats to the "Plano Real" economic stablization plan continues to be the bleeding in public accounts, with this year's operational deficit seen at 3.16 percent of GDP, according to a Reuters survey.

In a move underlining its commitment to fiscal discipline, the government Wednesday published a decree assigning all privatization receipts to the retirement of Brazil's massive stock of public sector debt.
Pedro Parente, executive secretary of the Finance Ministry, said the decree proved Cardoso's team was committed to reducing the public sector fiscal deficit.

Quoted by the private Invest News agency, Parente said the measure would result in lower interest rates and in a 30-40 percent reduction in the net debt stock, currently hanging at around 280 billion reais, or 34 percent of GDP.

The decree was seen by Brasilia watchers as a rebuff of Communications Minister Sergio Motta, who sent shock waves through regional bolsas Tuesday after criticizing the Central Bank and calling for privatization receipts to be spent on social projects.

Motta's remarks, which suggested a split in the government over policy, accentuated an already-steep plunge in Brazilian stocks, which began last Friday amid nervousness sparked by devaluations in Thailand and the Philippines.
